extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of constitutional design; readers of political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive principles for constitutional design: how to secure liberty and justice through laws, separation of powers, bicameral legislatures, and institutional checks that take human nature into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed constitution and stated laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither liberty nor justice can be secured, nor the prosperity of a nation promoted, but by a fixed constitution of government, and stated laws, known and obeyed by all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that a society needs a permanent, known body of laws (a fixed constitution) rather than rule by the arbitrary will of rulers; without such laws government becomes 'the government of mere will and pleasure.' Stable, known laws are a prerequisite for uninterrupted enjoyment of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberty as self-government by laws of one's own making
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil liberty is 'the power of a civil society to govern itself, by its own discretion, or by laws of its own making, by the majority, in a collective body, or by fair representation' (Dr. Price's definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition links liberty to the ability of a people to make and be governed by their own laws (majority or representative consent). The text also records objections (e.g., that unanimous or majority-made laws can still be unjust) and therefore suggests this definition must be supplemented by other safeguards (e.g., protection of individual rights/public good).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal laws made by common consent (legitimate government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimate government consists in the dominion of equal laws, made with common consent, and not in the dominion of any men over other men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republican writers' standard: laws should be equal and arise from common consent (majority/general will). The text cautions, however, that even 'equal laws' enacted by a majority may oppress minorities—thus equality of form does not guarantee justice of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government of laws, not of men
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-ordered commonwealth is described as 'an empire of laws and not of men' — laws should prevail rather than the arbitrary commands of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (Aristotle, Livy, Harrington, Sidney) are used to support the principle that laws must govern. The text also notes the paradox that laws are made by men and so require institutional constraints and repair when abused; the principle demands mechanisms to keep laws authoritative and immune from personal caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of legislative power: bicameralism and additional branches
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a necessity for two assemblies in the legislature, as well as a third branch, to defend the executive authority and secure liberty and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues for splitting legislative power (e.g., house of representatives and senate) and for a separate executive (governor), to produce wise and equal laws, avoid concentration, and provide internal checks (division and choosing). The Senate's role is framed as deliberative/counsel rather than unilateral lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of authority in a single assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: A single assembly with all authority will, on its first day, tend to become an aristocracy, then an oligarchy, divide into parties, and ultimately exclude the people or produce a victorious leader who governs arbitrarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an anti-pattern, centralizing all legislative power in one assembly is predicted to lead to faction, domination by a few families, hereditary power, or eventual tyranny. Constitutional design should therefore avoid vesting all authority in one body to prevent these paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power should be a check to power
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent abuse of power, 'by the very disposition of things, power should be a check to power' (Montesquieu): institutions must be arranged so different powers constrain each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses this as a fundamental design rule: create structural checks and balances so that ambition and authority in one organ are checked by others—implementing separation of powers and mutual restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must assume flawed human nature and passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional design must assume human weakness: passions like love of gold, praise, and ambition strengthen with indulgence and lead to abuse of power; men are apt to abuse power when unchecked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because human nature inclines toward accumulation of power and growing appetite for authority, institutional rules should limit and check power rather than rely on the virtue of officeholders; the text cites many authorities (Machiavel, Montesquieu, Swift, etc.) to justify precautionary design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws intended to guard against what men may do
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are intended 'not to trust to what men will do, but to guard against what they may do' (Junius): anticipate the mischiefs men are capable of and constrain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion frames laws as defensive instruments—anticipatory protections against predictable abuses—so designers should craft laws to forestall harm rather than assume benevolent behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as deliberative counsellors, not sole lawgivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate (or the small council of the wise) is 'not to be commanders, but counsellors of the people'—their decrees are not called laws but are maturely framed proposals to be offered to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional practice: reserve debate and careful deliberation to a smaller body that proposes measures, while ultimate enactment involves concurrence of the people or another assembly. This division (divide/choose) is used to secure wiser legislation and prevent hasty or self-interested lawmaking by a single body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special magistrates to protect subordinate estates (tribunes etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical practice shows creation of officers (e.g., tribunes) with privileges and authority to secure the rights of plebeians and curb the influence of patricians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design may require specific offices or protections for vulnerable groups or estates to rebalance power and prevent domination by elite classes; mechanisms can include vetoes, protective powers, or institutional representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence and continuity of laws to secure liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no uninterrupted enjoyment of liberty, nor any good government in society, without laws or where standing laws do not govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that laws must not only exist but be stable and continuously enforced; sudden repeal or absence of laws would produce disorder and insecurity of person and property. Thus, constitutional arrangements should promote longevity and predictability of legal rules.
